# HRB achieves major CRISPR breakthrough: first- ever regeneration of strawberries from gene- edited single cells
...
Hudson River Biotechnology (HRB), based in Wageningen, The Netherlands, announces a milestone achievement: the world’s first successful regeneration of strawberry plants from gene edited single cells using its proprietary CRISPR workflow (TiGER).
...
Gene editing technology offers a promising solution for quickly introducing desired genetic traits into strawberries.
The industry previously lacked an effective gene editing workflow that does not introduce foreign DNA or lead to plants with inconsistently edited cells (chimeras)– until now.
In response to this global challenge, HRB’s breakthrough offers a timely solution.
The TiGER workflow, which generates new plant varieties derived from a single, gene-edited cell, includes automated screening for thousands of regeneration conditions to identify the right combination for each crop/variety and it is proven to be both a scalable and effective method for fast-tracking the market introduction of valuable traits for different crops.
The dedication and expertise of HRB’s R&D team have been key in reaching this breakthrough that marks a world-first for strawberry, a notoriously recalcitrant crop and finally unlocks the potential for rapidly improving fruit flavor, nutritional value, and sustainability.
This not only adds a significant milestone to HRB’s extensive crop portfolio, which includes over 12 species, but also aligns with a broader vision in which all crops can benefit from CRISPR technology.
“Our success with strawberries is a significant advancement in agricultural biotechnology, paving the way for improved breeding and cultivation practices for berry crops.
Moving forward, HRB is keen to collaborate with industry partners to translate these scientific breakthroughs into practical solutions for farmers and consumers alike”, says Ferdinand Los, co-founder and CEO of HRB.

HRB is an independent technology provider focused on crop improvement through biotechnology to address the demands of a resilient, sustainable bioeconomy.
Specialized in CRISPR-based plant breeding and efficient smart delivery systems, HRB aims to enhance plant quality and yields while minimizing environmental impact.
By partnering with industry leaders, HRB contributes to more efficient and sustainable agriculture.

# Plantik and Hudson River Biotechnology team up to de-risk heat-tolerant strawberries
Plantik Biosciences and Hudson River Biotechnology are partnering to develop heat tolerance in crops, with the goal of producing a validated heat-tolerance trait any strawberry breeder can license.
By combining heat-tolerant targets identified and validated by Plantik in tomatoes with "transgene-free" strawberry genome editing methods developed by Hudson River, the companies hope to turn trait discoveries into "improved strawberry varieties."
Validation trials are already underway.
According to Plantik cofounder and CEO Ying Shao, heat tolerance is "a must-have trait for many crops across the globe" thanks to the rise in extreme heat events worldwide in recent years.
Strawberries are among the most exposed crops, as these high temperatures disrupt flowering and fruit set, and damage overall fruit quality.
France-based Plantik employs its ATLANTIS machine learning platform to search "the dark genome," the regulatory stretches of DNA in plants that switch genes on and off.
It then edits those regions without inserting any foreign DNA, allowing plant breeders to fast-track development of crops.
Plantik's first product is a heat-tolerant tomato, which the company claims it developed in about 12 months instead of the five to eight years required by traditional breeding.
The company is currently running demonstrations across greenhouses and fields in the US and Belgium.
"We have now worked on this trait in multiple tomato crops, from lab tomatoes to now commercial hybrids," says Shao.
"Overall, we see that in the real conditions, the material also performs much better in terms of yield preservation under high heat."

# Hudson River Biotechnology and PBL Collaboration
We are pleased to announce a collaboration between Hudson River Biotechnology and PBL Technology focused on accelerating deployment of CRISPR-enabled traits in tomato and strawberry breeding programs.
A major bottleneck in commercial CRISPR breeding is often not identifying interesting traits, but efficiently deploying them into elite breeding germplasm and active breeding pipelines.
Through this collaboration, validated trait concepts and technologies from PBL’s portfolio will be combined with HRB’s BioMaas™ deployment platform for transgene-free CRISPR breeding and single-cell regeneration.
Together, we aim to help breeders access and implement new traits more rapidly and practically within commercial breeding programs.
We look forward to working together to accelerate innovation in tomato and strawberry breeding.

# Hudson River Biotechnology opens up new laboratory
**Hudson River Biotechnology (HRB) opens up a state-of-the-art laboratory in Wageningen to facilitate its ground-breaking research in precision plant breeding.**
Wageningen, 18 December 2018 – Following the global surge in CRISPR investments and research, HRB is pleased to announce the opening of its new 150m2 laboratory.
As one of the few European companies fully dedicated to gene-editing and precision plant breeding, HRB is pleased to take this next important step in the evolution of the company and strengthen the agricultural R&D eco-system in Europe.
HRB is a young and highly innovative agricultural biotech company located in Wageningen(Netherlands).
HRB applies novel breeding techniques such as **CRISPR ** to develop new plant traits and has exclusive access to a novel genetic target identification platform, called **SuRE **(licensed from Amsterdam-based partner company Gen-X).
HRB genetically optimizes crops to increase yields, improve disease resistance & nutritional value.
The company has an internal R&D pipeline for development of *novel platform technologies * and varieties with new traits.
In addition, HRB uses their molecular breeding and target identification expertise to accelerate breeding efforts in co-development with plant breeders, seed companies and natural ingredient producers of all sizes.
Combined, these efforts ultimately contribute to solving global food challenges such as the need for improved nutritional value or reduced pesticide use.
“We look forward to continue the rapid expansion of our company through this new lab” says Rudi Ariaans, CEO and HRB co-founder.
...
In the new laboratory, HRB can deploy a range of activities in plant tissue and protoplast culture, genetics (DNA and RNA work), and protein biology.
This enables HRB to effectively perform all the required steps in, for example, a CRISPR project, including discovery of genetic targets, in-house production of CRISPR proteins and guide RNAs, plant transfection and regeneration, and genetic testing.

# Hudson River Biotechnology and Pairwise Sign Fulcrum® Licensing Agreement
...
Hudson River expands their plant genome editing offering with access to Pairwise's plant gene editing platform
Wageningen, Netherlands and Durham, N.C. — May 26, 2026 — Hudson River Biotechnology (Hudson River) and Pairwise have signed a licensing agreement giving Hudson River access to the Fulcrum® plant gene editing platform.
Hudson River will integrate Fulcrum® tools into its editing services, which it offers to crop improvement customers working in vegetable, soft fruit, and other species.
Hudson River is an independent plant biotechnology company based in the Netherlands, specializing in genome editing, plant regeneration and trait development.
A Fulcrum® license gives Hudson River access to a broader set of editing tools, complementing their established BioMaas workflow.
"Our customers increasingly recognize genome editing as a crucial part of their breeding tools and come to us for our ability to apply this technology in a transgene-free manner directly in elite lines and flexible partnership models,” said Lotte Westerhof, CSO of Hudson River.
“Fulcrum® expands the editing toolbox we can offer, enabling us to support a broader range of applications and opportunities for our customers."
"Partnerships like this one are how Fulcrum® reaches more breeders and more crops," said Ian Miller, COO of Pairwise.
"We’re excited to work with Hudson River extending our platform for specialty crops where their customers are already active — accelerating the delivery of beneficial crops to agriculture."
Fulcrum® is Pairwise's integrated plant gene editing platform, encompassing gene editing tools, enzymes, and trait libraries that enable precise changes across a wide range of crop species.
The platform is developed and proven in Pairwise's own breeding programs and is made available to partners and licensees worldwide.

Plant genome-editing technology company Hudson River and plant engineering company Plantik announced a partnership to bring heat tolerance into commercial strawberries.

Hudson River’s BioMaas platform enables breeders to access its advanced genome-editing capabilities without having to build the R&D and technology in-house.
Throughout this collaboration, BioMaas will act as a bridge between trait innovators and breeders – helping trait companies translate their discoveries into crop-specific applications, while giving breeders an accessible route to valuable new traits.
Through BioMaas, strawberry breeders will be able to access unique and proprietary traits from specialized discovery companies such as Plantik, helping them expand and accelerate their innovation pipelines.
The partnership will tackle the heat tolerance challenge in strawberries as a starting point before applying it in other crops.
*″This collaboration is a perfect example of how trait knowledge can be leveraged from one crop to another, without the trait needing to be present in the breeder’s germplasm or lengthy backcrossing and selection.

# Plantik and Hudson River Target Heat-Tolerant Strawberries
## The companies are combining genome editing and machine learning to develop a heat-tolerance trait that strawberry breeders could license
** martes 29 de septiembre de 2026 - 16:07
**Plantik Biosciences and Hudson River Biotechnology have partnered to develop heat-tolerant strawberries, combining Plantik’s trait discovery technology with Hudson River’s transgene-free genome-editing methods.** The companies aim to validate a heat-tolerance trait that strawberry breeders could license and incorporate into commercial varieties, with validation trials already underway.
According to AgFunderNews, the collaboration will initially focus on strawberries, one of the crops exposed to rising temperatures because extreme heat can disrupt flowering and fruit set while reducing overall fruit quality.
The project builds on work already carried out by Plantik in tomatoes.
The France-based company uses its **ATLANTIS machine-learning platform** to explore regulatory regions of plant DNA that control how genes are switched on and off.
Plantik then edits those regions without inserting foreign DNA.
Plantik’s first product is a **heat-tolerant tomato**, which the company says it developed in approximately 12 months, compared with the five to eight years typically required through traditional breeding.
Demonstrations are currently taking place in greenhouses and fields in the United States and Belgium.
“We have now worked on this trait in multiple tomato crops, from lab tomatoes to now commercial hybrids,” Plantik cofounder and CEO Ying Shao told AgFunderNews.
“Overall, we see that in the real conditions, the material also performs much better in terms of yield preservation under high heat.”
The next challenge is transferring that approach to strawberries.
Hudson River Biotechnology will contribute its **BioMaas genome-editing platform**, which is designed to give breeders access to editing technologies without requiring them to build costly research and development capabilities internally.
Hudson River CEO Fernando Los said the company has developed technical capabilities that allow new traits to be introduced into tomatoes and strawberries in a matter of months.
In the partnership, Plantik will identify the genomic regions associated with heat tolerance, while Hudson River will carry out the required edits in strawberry plants.
Strawberries present a greater technical challenge than tomatoes because of their genetic complexity.
“Strawberry is a different story from tomato because it’s genetically much more complex,” Los said.
“It’s an octoploid species rather than a diploid.
Propagation is normally done clonaly, so you cannot create seeds; you have to work directly in relevant commercial germplasm, which are all things that we can do.”
The collaboration is designed to reduce the technical and financial risks faced by breeders seeking to introduce complex traits.
...
“If you reduce the failure rate from 90% to maybe 10% for a breeder, that’s a very good proposition to offer them.”
The companies ultimately want to produce a **validated heat-tolerance trait available for licensing to strawberry breeders**, allowing the technology to reach multiple commercial varieties rather than remaining tied to a single product.
...
For strawberries, improving tolerance to high temperatures could help preserve flowering, fruit development, quality and yields during periods of heat stress.
Strawberries are only the starting point.
Plantik and Hudson River plan to apply the same model to other crops and are inviting companies to bring additional trait challenges for strawberry varieties.
If the validation process succeeds, the partnership could create a pathway for breeders to access **genome-editing technology and climate-resilience traits** without developing the entire technological platform themselves, accelerating the introduction of new varieties designed for hotter growing conditions.

# French-Dutch partnership tackles heat tolerance in strawberries
October 12 , 2026
...
To address this, genetics technology firm Hudson River and engineering French company Plantik are combining gene-editing and elite-germplasm technologies to develop strawberries that can better withstand heat stress.
First commercial field trials are slated for spring and summer 2028.
The European firm’s co-founder and CEO Ying Shao told **FreshFruitPortal.com** that her team identified a **tomato genetic region associated with heat tolerance**, which provided the starting point.
“[The genetic region] is very well conserved across species, which gives us a strong shortcut in terms of where to look in the strawberry genome,” she said.
Plantik’s proprietary cloud data infrastructure and machine learning platform ATLANTIS has been pivotal to the work, Shao added.
“Using ATLANTIS, we are able to identify additional, adjacent target regions that also ranked high according to our algorithm and demonstrated high potential,” she said.
“This combination of a conserved primary target plus newly discovered adjacent targets gives us confidence that the trait will translate effectively.”
...
## Beyond heat tolerance
Fruit set is a critical production phase, and **heat can significantly interfere** with it, Shao explained.
That is why Plantik plans to evaluate several strawberry performance measures in upcoming trials slated for 2028.
“Beyond yield, fruit quality may also be altered under heat stress, including berry size shrinking and the sugar content being affected, which is particularly important for consumers in certain markets,” the CEO noted.
Shao said their approach aims to create a **conditional response to heat stress** while minimizing potential effects on normal plant development.
“The goal is for the plant to have a better mechanism to fight heat **only when the stressor is present, throughout its lifecycle**,” Shao said.
“When heat stress isn't present, the plant develops and behaves just like the unedited plant.”
Shao stressed that the company also plans to use the technology to reduce the likelihood of unintended effects associated with altering genes, and that other commodities may soon benefit from the process.
...
### Hudson River focuses on elite germplasm
Meanwhile, in Wageningen, Netherlands, Hudson River is tackling the issue directly at its genetic core.
The firm uses its BioMaas platform, an advanced, DNA-free plant genome-editing system to refine and enhance elite commercial varieties.
Chief Science Officer Lotte Westerhof explained to FreshFruitPortal.com that the time savings compared with conventional crossing and backcrossing depend on crop genetics and generation length.
In tomatoes, however, the company estimates that direct editing of elite germplasm can take **two to three times less time than introducing the same trait through conventional breeding.**
For crops with more complex genetics or longer generation cycles, Westerhof said the advantage could exceed tenfold.
“BioMaas allows us to introduce the desired change directly into the elite variety, avoiding the repeated crossing and selection needed to recover the original genetic background,” she said.
For strawberries, the executive said **Hudson River has tested more than 30 genotypes through its platform ** and has developed methods to address differences in regeneration efficiency among commercial varieties.
“One of the key elements is our **proprietary hydrogel technology**, which provides a highly supportive environment for individual protoplasts to re-enter the cell cycle and develop into callus,” Westerhof explained.
The company combines that technology with its accumulated knowledge of regeneration parameters to work across a wider range of commercial strawberry germplasm, she said.
Both companies expect regulatory requirements to remain smooth sailing.
Westerhof said the United States already has regulatory pathways for many transgene-free edited crops, while Europe is developing a framework for qualifying Category 1 New Genomic Technique (NGT-1) plants.
The BioMaas pipeline could eventually extend beyond heat tolerance.
Westerhof said the **platform is intended to address drought tolerance, disease resistance, yield stability, quality, and shelf life**, with market needs determining further priorities.

hits.title: Two Biotechs Edit Strawberries' "Dark Genome" to Survive Hotter Summers
hits.snippet:
# Two Biotechs Edit Strawberries’ “Dark Genome” to Survive Hotter Summers
**29 September 2026, Netherlands:** Two European agricultural biotech companies, Plantik Biosciences of France and Hudson River Biotechnology of the Netherlands, announced on September 28 that they are extending a gene-editing partnership from tomatoes into strawberries, targeting heat tolerance as extreme temperature events become more frequent across major growing regions.
The announcement was first reported by AgFunderNews, and validation trials on the edited strawberry material are already underway.
The two companies bring complementary pieces of the same puzzle.
Plantik, based at the Genopole biotech cluster near Paris, has built a machine learning platform called ATLANTIS that scans what scientists call the “dark genome,” the large share of a plant’s DNA that does not directly code for proteins but instead controls when, where and how strongly nearby genes switch on.
Rather than searching for a single gene to disable or insert, ATLANTIS is designed to identify small tweaks to these regulatory regions that adjust a plant’s existing traits without introducing foreign DNA.
Hudson River Biotechnology, based at Wageningen Campus in the Netherlands, supplies the execution side through its BioMaas platform, which performs the actual genome edits in crop tissue using transgene-free methods, meaning the final plant carries no inserted genetic material from another species, only altered versions of its own DNA sequence.
...
## From Tomato to Strawberry
The strawberry project builds directly on an earlier collaboration between the two companies that produced a heat-tolerant tomato line.
According to the companies, that tomato was developed in roughly 12 months using the ATLANTIS-BioMaas combination, compared with the five to eight years a conventional breeding program would typically need to introduce and stabilize a similar trait.
The edited tomato has since shown improved yield preservation under high-heat conditions in real-world trial settings, according to the companies, giving them a proof point to apply the same approach to a new crop.
...
## Live Newsroom
Neither company disclosed financial terms of the expanded partnership or named specific funding behind the strawberry work.
Hudson River chief executive Fernando Los and chief of staff Lotte Westerhof, both quoted in the original report, described the company’s ability to execute complex regulatory-region edits in a matter of months once a target is identified, underscoring that the current bottleneck in this style of crop improvement is increasingly the target-discovery step that ATLANTIS is built to speed up, rather than the editing itself.
The approach illustrated by this partnership, editing regulatory DNA rather than protein-coding genes, is part of a broader shift in plant biotechnology that regulators in several markets, including the European Union and India, have begun treating differently from conventional transgenic GM crops, since no foreign gene is inserted into the final plant.
That distinction matters commercially: precision-bred or gene-edited varieties of this kind can often reach farmers faster and with a lighter regulatory path than first-generation GM crops, which is part of why venture-backed biotechs are racing to apply the model across specialty and fruit crops, not just the commodity row crops that dominated the first wave of agricultural biotechnology.
For seed companies, nurseries and horticultural input suppliers serving strawberry and other high-value fruit sectors in India, the Gulf and Southeast Asia, where rising temperatures are already squeezing flowering and fruit-set windows, a validated method for compressing trait development from years to months is a preview of how climate-adaptation traits may increasingly reach the market.
